title: The DAO and the order of two lines

blocks.heading: The DAO and the order of two lines
text: On 17 June 2016 somebody began emptying a contract holding over 12 million ether.
No key was stolen. No cryptography broke. They used the published interface, correctly.

blocks.heading: A fund with no directors
text: The DAO took money from thousands of people - roughly 150 million dollars at the prices of the time - and let token holders vote on where it went.
Anyone outvoted could **split**: leave, taking their share of the ether with them.

blocks.heading: Splitting does three things
text: Check that you have a balance. Send you the ether. Set your balance to zero.
All three are correct. Only the order is wrong.

blocks.label: check, interaction, effect - in that order

blocks.heading: Sending ether is calling code
text: This is the fact the whole incident rests on. An Ethereum address may be a contract, and sending it ether runs its code.
So line two does not simply transfer value. It hands control to the recipient, in the middle of a function, before line three has run.

blocks.heading: So the attacker called back in

blocks.alt: Four nested calls, each checking a balance of 100 and sending 100, with the line that zeroes the balance never reached
blocks.caption: Each frame passes the same check, because the line that would fail it is still waiting below.

blocks.question: The second call checks the balance and passes. Why? The money has already been sent.
answer: Sent, but not recorded. The subtraction is on the line after the send, and that line has not executed yet - the function is suspended at line two, four levels deep.
The contract's memory of what it owes you is only updated when it gets around to it, and the attacker never lets it get around to it.

blocks.title: Checks, effects, interactions
text: Write the state **before** handing control to anyone. Move line three above line two and the entire incident does not happen.
That is the whole fix, and it was known practice before June 2016.

blocks.heading: About 3.6 million ether left
text: It went into a "child DAO" - a copy of the same contract, which inherited the same **28-day** holding period before anything could be withdrawn.
The attacker's money was frozen by the attacker's own exploit. That accident is the only reason there was time to argue.

blocks.heading: And then people voted
text: A hard fork at block **1,920,000** moved the funds to a recovery contract. Most of the network took it.
Nodes that refused kept running the original history. That chain is **Ethereum Classic** - the one attacked in lesson 17.
Nothing in Ethereum malfunctioned. The EVM ran the contract exactly as written, which is what it promises.
"The code is the agreement" was tested against 150 million dollars, and what actually settled it was a fortnight of argument and a coordinated software release.

blocks.heading: Why the obvious fix went stale
text: For years the advice was to use `transfer()`, which forwards only 2,300 gas - too little to re-enter.
Then gas costs were repriced, 2,300 stopped being enough for legitimate recipients, and contracts relying on the stipend broke. Ordering is durable; gas allowances are not.

blocks.heading: One sentence worth keeping
text: On a chain where sending money executes the recipient's code, the order of your statements is a security boundary.
Next: what a token actually is, which is less than almost anyone assumes.
